A.explanation: Area 1 is positive displacement and area 2 is displacement in the opposite direction, so net displacement is their signed sum.

B.explanation: Dividing by 2 would give an average of the two area magnitudes, not the signed area under the $v$-$t$ graph.

C.explanation: Adding the magnitudes gives total distance travelled, not total displacement which must subtract motion back past the start.

D.explanation: This reverses the signs, treating the below-axis motion as positive and the main forward motion as negative.

hints: Notice that area 1 lies above the time axis where velocity is positive, while area 2 lies below the time axis where velocity is negative.
Recall that displacement is the signed area under a velocity-time graph, so motion in opposite directions contributes with opposite signs.
Compare adding the two magnitudes, which gives distance, with subtracting the return part to leave net change of position.
walkthrough: Identify the graph features: area 1 is bounded by positive velocity and the time axis, area 2 is bounded by negative velocity and the time axis.
State the rule: for a velocity-time graph, displacement $= $ area under the graph, with area above the time axis positive and area below the time axis negative.
Apply the sign rule: the forward displacement is $+\text{area 1}$ and the return displacement is $-\text{area 2}$ where area 2 means the magnitude.
Combine for net change of position: total displacement $= \text{area 1} - \text{area 2}$.
Note that $\text{area 1} + \text{area 2}$ would be total distance, which ignores direction. This is option A.
